answers.q: How much electricity does one ChatGPT question use?

guess.prompt: One short ChatGPT question uses about as much electricity as…
options: A US home for a day

answers.result: About 2% of a phone charge
answers.reveal: One phone charge, about 19 Wh, is 10 to 80 short questions, depending on whose figure you use.
answers.answer: About 2% of a phone charge. OpenAI says an average question uses 0.34 Wh. Other published figures are 0.24 Wh (Google, for Gemini) and 1.86 Wh (one large open model, estimated by MIT Technology Review). They measure different things, so they can’t be ranked. Pasting in a long document can use about 7 to 120 times more (Epoch AI), and thinking modes about 30 times more on average (Hugging Face, open models).

Much of the monitor’s estimate rests on forecast data-centre load, and the monitor itself calls the accuracy of those forecasts highly questionable.
The monitor’s figures cover the capacity market. Maryland’s consumer advocate says data centres also raise energy and transmission costs; Hum hasn’t sourced a figure for those.
Berkeley Lab warns the past pattern (more demand, lower prices) may not hold as data-centre growth speeds up.

answers.q: Will AI cut more emissions than it causes?

answers.heardFrom: a common argument for building more AI

That is a scenario, not a measurement. The IEA says there is “currently no momentum” behind that uptake, that rebound effects could undercut the gains, and that AI is “not a silver bullet”. Data centres’ own emissions are already happening.

answers.share: Will AI cut more emissions than it causes? In an IEA scenario, yes: around 5% of energy-related emissions in 2035 if AI tools are widely used. But that’s a forecast, and the IEA calls AI “not a silver bullet”.

answers.q: Why do people near data centres hear a constant hum, and how loud can it be?

answers.reveal: A noise expert says people call 55 to 65 decibels no louder than conversation. The trouble, residents say, is that it never stops.
answers.answer: Mostly cooling. Data centres run cooling machinery night and day, and in Chandler, Arizona, residents traced a high-pitched hum to one centre’s air conditioning. US limits are local. Fairfax County, Virginia, allows 60 dBA of steady noise in residential areas by day and 55 at night; since 2024 a new data centre must show, with a noise study at full cooling load, that it complies. Chandler requires new ones to be no louder than the area’s measured background. Both set daytime hours for routine tests of backup generators.
answers.world: Near a cluster of Amazon data centres in Prince William County, Virginia, measurements found the noise below the county’s 60-decibel daytime limit about half the time. Residents still said the constant drone, especially at night, cost them sleep. Amazon was muffling its cooling equipment, the local paper reported.
dontknow: Nobody publishes a count of how many people live within earshot of a data centre.
Hum hasn’t found a published follow-up on whether Amazon’s new fans and shrouds quietened Great Oak.
Rules keep changing: in 2023 Prince William County still exempted air-conditioning noise, and was weighing whether to change that.
answers.share: Why data centres hum: their cooling runs night and day. Fairfax County, Virginia, caps steady noise in residential areas at 55 dBA at night; Chandler, Arizona, says new ones can’t be louder than the background.

answers.q: Will more efficient AI chips fix AI’s energy problem?
answers.heard: “More efficient AI chips will fix AI’s energy problem.”
answers.result: Not on their own
answers.reveal: Each AI answer uses far less energy than it did, but use is growing faster, so the total keeps rising.

Efficiency is improving fast: the IEA says energy per AI task has fallen at least tenfold a year recently, and Google says its median Gemini text prompt used 33x less energy over 12 months. But use grows faster. Google processed 50 times more tokens a month than a year before, and data centres’ electricity consumption grew 17% in 2025. Even in the IEA’s High Efficiency case, data centres use around 970 TWh in 2035, about double 2025.

answers.q: Does big tech really run on 100% renewable energy?
answers.result: On paper over a year, yes. Hour by hour, no
answers.reveal: Google matched 100% of its 2025 electricity use with renewable purchases over the year, but hour by hour its data centres and offices ran on about 65% carbon-free energy, by its own figures.
answers.answer: Partly. The 100% is a yearly sum on paper: companies buy clean power or certificates equal to the electricity they use. Google says it matched 100% of its 2025 consumption this way. Counted hour by hour on each local grid, its data centres and offices ran on about 65% carbon-free energy. Google itself says firms with a 100% annual match still use fossil power when or where clean power isn’t available. Counted on the grids it drew from, its electricity emissions were about 5.4 times what it reports after purchases.
answers.world: Worldwide, the grids data centres draw from supply about 30% of their electricity from coal and 26% from gas, with about 27% from renewables, by the IEA’s estimate. A peer-reviewed Princeton study of the western US grid found that matching a year’s use has minimal impact on long-run emissions, while matching it hour by hour can cut them significantly.
answers.why: The purchases are real, and the yearly sum adds up. But it isn’t the electricity the data centres draw from the grid each hour. Another study estimates that if certificate use keeps its trend, 42% of companies’ promised cuts in electricity emissions won’t be real-world cuts.
dontknow: These are the companies’ own figures. Hum found no independent hour-by-hour measurement of their clean power.
Google publishes an hourly figure. Many companies don’t, so their 100% claims can only be checked as a yearly sum.
Google’s electricity demand grew 37% in 2025. It doesn’t say how much of that growth is AI.
answers.share: “100% renewable” is a yearly sum on paper. Google matched 100% of its 2025 electricity that way, but hour by hour on local grids it ran on about 65% carbon-free energy, by its own figures.

answers.q: Should I stop using ChatGPT to help the planet?
answers.heard: “Using ChatGPT is bad for the planet.”
answers.heardFrom: said at school, at parties and online
answers.result: Small for you, big in total
answers.reveal: A typical user’s year of questions makes about 0.2 kg of CO₂, roughly half a mile in a US car. The total is what’s large: data centres used about 485 TWh in 2025.
answers.answer: Partly. One person’s share is small: a typical user’s year of ChatGPT questions makes about 0.2 kg of CO₂ by Hum’s sums from OpenAI’s figures, roughly what an average US car emits in half a mile (US EPA). Even 50 questions a day is about 7 miles of driving. Some uses weigh more: one short AI video clip used about 90 Wh in a Hugging Face test, as much as about 260 short questions. The large part is the total, and it’s growing fast.
answers.world: All the world’s data centres consumed about 485 TWh of electricity in 2025, and the IEA expects about 950 TWh by 2030. Electricity use by AI-focused data centres grew 50% in 2025. How much CO₂ that makes depends on where the power comes from: the IEA expects renewables to meet half of the growth.
answers.why: It’s true of the total, not of one person’s text questions. The total depends on billions of users, heavy uses like video, and the power behind the data centres.
dontknow: OpenAI gives only an average per question and hasn’t published how it’s measured.
Nobody publishes how use is spread across people, so a typical user is an average.
The grids behind ChatGPT’s data centres aren’t published, so the world average stands in.
Training, chips and buildings aren’t counted in one person’s share.
answers.share: Is using ChatGPT bad for the planet? Partly: a typical user’s year of questions makes about 0.2 kg of CO₂, roughly half a mile in a US car (Hum’s sums). The total is the big part: data centres used about 485 TWh in 2025 (IEA).

answers.q: Which uses more electricity: training AI, or people using it?

guess.prompt: Where a company has published the split, which took more of its machine-learning energy?

answers.result: Using it, where anyone has measured
answers.reveal: At Google, about three fifths of machine-learning energy went on use and two fifths on training, in the three years before 2022.
answers.answer: Using it, in the little data there is. Training is a big one-off; use (called inference) repeats with every question. Google said machine learning was 10% to 15% of its energy, about three fifths of it for use and two fifths for training. AWS estimated inference at 80 to 90% of machine-learning cloud demand. Researchers measuring open models found use overtakes training after hundreds of millions to tens of billions of answers: 200 to 590 million for Hugging Face’s BLOOMz models.
answers.world: Use adds up fast: ChatGPT alone got about 2.6 billion messages a day by July 2025, by Hum’s sums from OpenAI’s count. All the world’s data centres together used about 485 TWh in 2025.
answers.why: Training is paid once per model, though each new model is trained again. Use keeps going for as long as people keep asking.
dontknow: No company has published a training versus use split since chatbots took off; Google’s is from before 2022.
OpenAI, Google and Anthropic don’t publish how much energy training their newest models took.
Splits are counted different ways: Meta put about one-third of its machine-learning carbon on use in a 2021 paper, counting data and storage alongside training.
answers.share: Where it’s been measured, using AI takes more energy than training it: about three fifths of Google’s machine-learning energy went on use (Google, 2022).
